language.script_notes: Malay (Bahasa Malaysia) in Latin script, very close to Indonesian but with some spelling/vocabulary differences; English widely used alongside. Street suffixes: Jalan, Lorong, Persiaran, Lebuh, Taman, Kampung. Chinese and Tamil script also visible on signage due to the country's large Chinese and Indian communities.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Often black, white, grey and red — Malaysian bollards commonly carry two red rectangles.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Simple post with two red reflective rectangles.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Black-and-white painted guardrails are common — a strong Malaysia tell.
road_furniture.line_paint: White outside/white inside lines; occasionally thick yellow lines running perpendicular to the road (rumble-style) and double solid white center lines, both relatively rare elsewhere in the world.
road_furniture.curb_style: Black-and-white painted kerbs common in towns and cities.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Street signs are often mounted on black-and-white striped poles. Petronas (the national oil company), Caltex, Petron and BHPetrol are common fuel-station brands.

architecture.roof_style: Varies — traditional Malay houses have steeply pitched roofs on stilts; mosques with domes and minarets are extremely common; multi-tiered roofs on older wooden mosques; Chinese temples with curved ornate roofs; modern high-rises in urban areas.
architecture.roof_material: Corrugated metal and clay tile; domed concrete roofing on mosques.
architecture.wall_construction: Concrete-block terrace houses and shophouses dominate towns and cities; traditional Malay stilt houses (kampung houses) in rural areas; colonial-era buildings in KL and Georgetown blend Mughal, Tudor and neo-Gothic influences.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Pastel-painted terraced houses and shophouses; white and green on mosques.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Mosques with domes and minarets in every town; Chinese temples and clan houses; colonial-era civic buildings; the Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur as an unmistakable landmark; kampung stilt houses.

nature.vegetation: Oil palm and rubber plantations cover enormous stretches of the countryside — long regular rows of trees are a defining national tell; dense tropical rainforest in the interior, especially on Borneo.
nature.terrain: Peninsular Malaysia has a mountainous spine (Titiwangsa Range) between flat coastal plains; Malaysian Borneo (Sabah and Sarawak) is mountainous in Sabah and flatter/riverine in Sarawak, with vast rainforest.
nature.climate_signature: Hot, humid tropical rainforest climate year-round; lush green vegetation nationwide.

vehicles.plate_color: White plates with black text; black areas divide the plate into TWO white sections (distinguishing it from Indonesia's three-section plates).
vehicles.plate_format: Letters followed by digits (e.g. 'WXX 1234'); the letter prefix indicates the state of registration (W = Kuala Lumpur, Q = Sarawak, S = Sabah).
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Perodua and Proton (Malaysia's national car brands) are disproportionately common and a strong national tell; motorbikes are widespread.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mostly Gen 3/4 in Peninsular Malaysia; more variable in Borneo.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Dense across Peninsular Malaysia; Sabah's coverage is largely mountain roads, and Sarawak's coverage is flatter but sparser.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared left-hand traffic, similar Latin-script Malay/Indonesian language, similar tropical vegetation and plantations
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Malaysian plates split into TWO white sections vs. Indonesia's three; Malaysia's black-and-white painted guardrails/kerbs and Perodua/Proton cars are strong tells; Indonesian signage commonly uses the abbreviated 'Jl.' for street.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared left-hand traffic and tropical peninsula vegetation near the border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Malaysian Latin-script Malay/English signage and mosques vs. Thailand's Thai script and Buddhist temples; plate formats also differ.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared left-hand traffic, Malay place names, similar tropical climate and shophouse/HDB-style architecture near Johor
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Singapore's road furniture and plates differ sharply (much tidier and more regulated); Singapore is a tiny city-state so any rural or plantation landscape is almost certainly Malaysia.
